18                THE SECRETARY:   Legislative 

19   Resolution Number 1058, by Senators Gianaris and 

20   Skelos, memorializing Governor Andrew M. Cuomo to 

21   proclaim March 2015 as Greek History Month in the 

22   State of New York, in conjunction with the 

23   commemoration of the 194th Anniversary of Greek 

24   Independence.

25                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator 


                                                                1301

 1   Gianaris.

 2                SENATOR GIANARIS:   Thank you, 

 3   Mr. President.  

 4                This is the time of year, my 

 5   colleagues, where Senator Skelos and I come 

 6   together and agree in a bipartisan manner on 

 7   major policy for the State of New York.  I'm not 

 8   talking about the budget; I'm talking about the 

 9   importance of Greek Independence Day and Greek 

10   History Month that we recognize here in the State 

11   of New York.  And today is in fact the 194th 

12   anniversary of Greek independence.  

13                Everyone I'm sure knows, just from 

14   their own educations, about the importance of 

15   ancient Greece to Western civilization -- the 

16   founders of democracy that we practice in this 

17   chamber, the contributions to science and 

18   education and culture, and even to this day, in 

19   the United States, the great importance that the 

20   Greek-American community plays.

21                I don't know because I haven't gone 

22   back throughout the hundreds of years of history 

23   in this Legislature, but I do believe, 

24   anecdotally, that we have more Greek-Americans 

25   elected in the State Legislature in New York 


                                                                1302

 1   right now than at any time in history.  We have 

 2   the two of us here in the Senate, four members in 

 3   the State Assembly.  And both parties, both 

 4   genders are represented.  

 5                And it's a testament to the 

 6   contributions of the Greek immigrants in the 

 7   United States and their successes in this 

 8   country.  My parents were, in fact, both 

 9   immigrants from Greece.  I know Senator Skelos's 

10   ancestry as well, I think it was his 

11   grandparents.  And a number of our colleagues in 

12   the Assembly share the story that so many of us 

13   do -- not just Greeks, but people who have had 

14   their parents and grandparents and others come 

15   from other countries around the world.  

16                I think Senator Griffo takes pride 

17   in being a part of what we call the Olive Caucus, 

18   so we have a kinship also with our Italian 

19   colleagues, because it's an immigrant story that 

20   we all share.  

21                And the fact we are able to come 

22   together for a brief moment in the middle of all 

23   the budget discussions and pause to reflect on 

24   that is something that I thank my colleagues for 

25   and appreciate the opportunity to speak on this

14                THE SECRETARY:   Legislative 

15   Resolution Number 1068, by Senator Martins, 

16   commemorating the 104th Anniversary of the 

17   Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire on March 25, 

18   2015.

19                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator 

20   Martins.

21                SENATOR MARTINS:   Thank you, 

22   Mr. President.  

23                Today we join with Workers 

24   United/SEIU and the New York City Fire Department 

25   in commemorating the 104th anniversary of the 


                                                                1304

 1   Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire.  

 2                We heard about this fire, we learned 

 3   about this fire and this tragedy in textbooks as 

 4   we were growing up.  One hundred forty-six people 

 5   died on the 8th, 9th, and 10th floors of this 

 6   building under deplorable conditions.  

 7                The fire started on the 8th floor -- 

 8   they were able to get out, everyone but one on 

 9   the 8th floor -- moved to the 10th floor, they 

10   were able to get out.  But nobody told anyone on 

11   the 9th floor.  And when they tried to get out -- 

12   there were two stairs.  One of the staircases 

13   opened in, so obviously they couldn't get the 

14   door open.  The second was locked because the 

15   owners didn't want to allow workers the 

16   opportunity to leave early.  One hundred 

17   forty-six women died, the youngest 14 years old. 

18                As they struggled with the fire, 

19   they got out on the ledges on the 9th floor 

20   waiting for the fire department to come.  But at 

21   the time, New York City's fire apparatus only 

22   reached the 6th floor.  A tremendous tragedy.  

23                And it marks one of those moments in 

24   our history, certainly a tragedy in New York 

25   City's history, that led to the labor movement.  


                                                                1305

 1   The changes that were brought about as a result 

 2   of this tragedy, the lessons that were learned as 

 3   a result of this tragedy are still with us today.  

 4                And that's why it's important that 

 5   we take the opportunity every year as a 

 6   legislative body to remember this, to remember 

 7   the tragedy and to understand the need to also 

 8   give thanks that we as a society have gotten 

 9   beyond this.  Through our efforts in labor, we 

10   have gotten beyond conditions that led to the 

11   possibility of 146 people dying in a fire.  

12   Again, the youngest was 14 years old.

13                So, Mr. President, we join today 

14   with the City of New York, with Workers 

15   United/SEIU, with the New York City Fire 

16   Department as we remember.  And we remember the 

17   lessons of that day, and we remember to thank 

18   labor for all they do.

19                And also it's a commitment from us 

20   as a body, it's a commitment from us as a state 

21   that we will continue to work with them to 

22   provide safeguards to ensure that labor in 

23   New York State is safe, or certainly as safe as 

24   it can be.

25                As a result of this tragedy, the 


                                                                1306

 1   Legislature formed a commission.  And as a result 

 2   of that commission, they had 64 suggestions or 

 3   recommendations.  Sixty of those were enacted 

 4   into law between 1911 and 1913.  

 5                Those laws mandated better building 

 6   access and egress -- no longer can doorways be 

 7   locked -- fireproofing requirements, sprinklers, 

 8   basic requirements of sprinklers in workplaces to 

 9   ensure that at the very least we're going to give 

10   people a fighting chance when there is a fire.  

11   Alarm systems, automatic sprinklers, as I said, 

12   and a limited number of hours for women and 

13   children in the workplace.  Remarkable 

14   achievements, things that we take for granted 

15   today, but unfortunately it took a tragedy 104 

16   years ago to bring it to fruition.  

17                So, Mr. President, thank you very 

18   much for the opportunity.  I thank my colleagues 

19   for joining with me in this resolution as we 

20   commemorate this significant moment in the labor 

21   movement, not only for the country but certainly 

22   here in New York State.  

23                Thank you.

24                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Thank 

25   you, Senator Martins.  


                                                                1307

 1                Senator Savino.

 2                SENATOR SAVINO:   Thank you, 

 3   Mr. President.  

 4                I thought I was going to be 

 5   following Senator Hoylman, in whose district the 

 6   Triangle Shirtwaist Factory is.

 7                I want to thank my colleague Senator 

 8   Martins, who's now the chair of the Labor 

 9   Committee, for continuing this tradition of 

10   recognizing and acknowledging that horrible 

11   tragedy at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory.  

12                Prior to us being here, this 

13   resolution was always presented by a former 

14   member of this body, Senator Maltese, whose 

15   grandmother and his aunt, I believe, were in that 

16   fire.

17                And there's also another fire that's 

18   being commemorated today.  In the City of 

19   New York there was a tragedy several years ago, 

20   about 25 years ago -- I'm not sure of the exact 

21   time -- the Happy Land fire.  Many of us remember 

22   that, where people were trapped in a fire in an 

23   unregulated nightclub.  Dozens of people perished 

24   there.  

25                And just the other day there was a 


                                                                1308

 1   horrible fire in I believe it was Senator 

 2   Felder's district, where seven children died.  

 3                So what is the connection between 

 4   all of these things?  Labor rights, fire 

 5   protection, public service.  In my opinion, all 

 6   those things are intertwined.  

 7                And here we are more than a hundred 

 8   years after the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, 

 9   where working people have made tremendous gains, 

10   largely because of the workers banding together 

11   for the purpose of improving workers' rights, 

12   advancing the issues that unions fought for prior 

13   to their being legal and after their being legal.  

14   And that's when we developed standards that we 

15   could all count on, whether they be in factories 

16   or they be in houses or they be in our fire 

17   departments.  

18                And here we are more than a hundred 

19   years later as we continue to see, in states 

20   across this country, where we have governors and 

21   the legislatures chipping away at those very 

22   protections that were meant to make sure we never 

23   had another Triangle Shirtwaist Factory.  Or 

24   these horrible tragedies where we have shortages 

25   of staff or we've taken away the expertise of our 


                                                                1309

 1   firefighters to recognize what is dangerous and 

 2   what isn't.  

 3                And so while we reflect on that day, 

 4   let us not forget that we could easily turn the 

 5   clock back and we could have Triangle Shirtwaist 

 6   Factories all over this country.

 7                So we have an obligation to 

 8   acknowledge what happened then and to make sure 

 9   that we do not undermine those advances, either 

10   in fire protection or in public service.  

11                Thank you, Senator Martins.  

12                Thank you, Mr. President.

13                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator 

14   Hoylman.

15                SENATOR HOYLMAN:   Thank you, 

16   Mr. President.  

17                I rise to thank my colleagues 

18   Senator Martins and Senator Savino for their 

19   leadership on labor issues over the years.  

20                And as was noted, the building of 

21   the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory is in my district 

22   at 29 Washington Place, just off of Washington 

23   Square Park.  And it's quite a serene place.  

24   You'd never know, walking along that cobblestone 

25   street just off of the square and tucked in into 


                                                                1310

 1   between university buildings, that such a tragedy 

 2   occurred there 104 years ago.  One hundred 

 3   forty-six garment workers, most of them new 

 4   immigrants from Italy, or Jewish from Eastern 

 5   Europe, 123 women.  

 6                And it's so important that we 

 7   remember what occurred then but also look at the 

 8   tragedy through the prism of the issues before us 

 9   today.  And whether it's immigrant rights and the 

10   anti-immigrant sentiment that exists in our 

11   country today, or the rights of farmworkers, the 

12   incidents of hate crimes, which are increasing in 

13   this nation and in this state, civil rights for 

14   people of all colors and creeds, sexual 

15   orientations, people who are transgender, or the 

16   rights of women to control their own bodies -- 

17   we've made so much progress, Mr. President, but 

18   we have so much yet to do.

19                So I join my colleagues in this 

20   historic commemoration and look forward to 

21   working them to make certain that we move forward 

22   with progress for all.

23                Thank you, Mr. President.

22                SENATOR KRUEGER:   Thank you, 

23   Mr. President.

24                The bill we have before us today is 

25   our first budget bill.  It is the General Debt 


                                                                1316

 1   Service Fund Budget Bill.  

 2                I've often pointed out we do budget 

 3   bills in a strange order in this house.  We tend 

 4   to do the revenue bill last, so we've spent all 

 5   the money before we pass a bill providing any 

 6   money for the state to function on.

 7                And we tend to do the debt service 

 8   bill first, also before we have completed any 

 9   other work on the budget.  

10                And yet it's very difficult to argue 

11   that we shouldn't all vote yes on the debt 

12   service bill, because to not, and to not ensure 

13   that the State of New York can continue its 

14   fiduciary responsibility to make payments on 

15   debt, would result in the State of New York not 

16   actually being able to go back to the market and 

17   borrow any more funds.  

18                So we need to vote yes on this bill, 

19   and we need to make sure it's on time.  But I 

20   also think it's important, while explaining my 

21   vote today, to remind everyone that we are a 

22   state that takes on an enormous amount of debt.  

23                In fiscal year 2015-2016, the total 

24   state debt-related service appropriations are 

25   $9.859 billion, including some contingency 


                                                                1317

 1   appropriations.  That brings our outstanding 

 2   state-related debt to the level of $56.9 billion, 

 3   or basically $60 billion through 3/31/16.

 4                It's an enormous amount of debt.  

 5   And it's important to remember the job of 

 6   government is to provide public services, 

 7   continue our infrastructure securely, raise 

 8   enough revenue to meet our expenses, including 

 9   the recognition that when we take on more and 

10   more debt, we have more and more interest 

11   payments and repayment obligations.

12                So sometimes people say simply:  Why 

13   do you need to tax us so much?  Why are you 

14   spending so much money?  I think it's valuable to 

15   remind them if we didn't raise money, raise 

16   revenue, if we didn't spend the money on 

17   important public services such as our schools and 

18   our police and our fire and our other public 

19   safety and our infrastructure, we wouldn't have a 

20   state any of us wanted to live in.

21                And a huge amount of our debt is to 

22   cover capital costs.  And I would just remind us 

23   this is the year where we need to deal with the 

24   five-year capital plans for transportation in 

25   this state, both DOT for roads and bridges, and 


                                                                1318

 1   MTA for public transportation in the 12 southern 

 2   counties.  And that's exactly what debt is 

 3   supposed to be for, taking on large capital 

 4   infrastructure costs.

 5                So I'm not saying we shouldn't have 

 6   debt.  I'm saying we should all be aware of it, 

 7   we should all recognize why we end up with such 

 8   enormous debt.  And we should recognize if we 

 9   don't make the investments in the infrastructure 

10   of this state to ensure that we have functioning 

11   water systems, sewage systems, roads, bridges, 

12   trains, subways, buses, then it almost doesn't 

13   matter what else we think we would like to do 

14   with our lives.  Because if we don't have all of 

15   that infrastructure in place, we don't have much 

16   of a future here.

17                So I would encourage all my 

18   colleagues to vote yes, but also to think about 

19   what we do in government and why it often 

20   involves such large distributions of money and 

21   the reason that governments need to go and borrow 

22   money.

23                Thank you, Mr. President.
